forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

summary.summary: Portsmouth ended the year with gross debt of £718m (including £56m of PFI) against investments of £230m — net debt £488m — and took no new borrowing at all, running £292m of internal borrowing instead while new money costs over 5%. Its borrowing need (CFR) is £1,010m, so £292m of real borrowing is deferred, not avoided; the council itself notes this needs ongoing monitoring as the need grows. Net treasury costs came in £0.01m under budget.

signals.headline: £292m of internal borrowing is deferred future borrowing — council flags it needs monitoring as the CFR grows
signals.why: When cash runs down or rates fall, this converts into real market borrowing demand.

signals.headline: No new borrowing; debt £718m within the £1,028m limit; treasury costs on budget
signals.why: Verified quiet on every compliance measure.

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth's temporary accommodation rose to 551 households in Q1 2026/27 from 459 a year earlier, driving £3.2m overspend
news_drafts.lead: Portsmouth's financial pressures are shifting from temporary budget gaps to structural demand growth that existing reserves cannot sustain. Temporary accommodation demand rose to 551 households in the first quarter of 2026/27, up from 459 a year earlier, driving a £3.2m overspend—the single largest pressure on the budget. Adult social care costs rose by £1.3m and children's placements by £0.86m, all driven by rising client volumes and placement costs. The council covered £7.5m of gross portfolio overspends by releasing £3.8m from contingency reserves and transferring £3m from earmarked reserves, leaving just £0.66m reported deficit. However, the deputy chief executive warned that "demand for services continues to place pressure...there remains longer term uncertainty relating to further increases in demand," signalling that budget pressures are unlikely to ease without structural change.
news_drafts.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/2027 (First Quarter) to end June 2026

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth faces three-year audit backlog and may not clear accounts until 2028
news_drafts.lead: Portsmouth's auditors have warned that the council will not achieve a fully unqualified audit opinion until after 2027/28, leaving its financial accounts lacking full independent verification for a third consecutive year. The external auditor, EY, issued a qualified opinion for 2024/25 because prior-year disclaimers had prevented sufficient audit evidence being gathered over major assets and reserves. During last year's audit, EY discovered a £30m error in how properties were valued in 2023/24, now flagged as a significant risk. Before rebuilding assurance can begin, the council must complete a comprehensive reconciliation of reserves across all disclaimed years. The timeline for recovery extends beyond the current financial year because properties are revalued on a five-year rolling programme, with the next full cycle not completing until 2027/28. EY says it may not move beyond a qualified opinion until after that date.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/2027 (First Quarter) to end June 2026
findings.headline: Treasury management underspend of £747,700 from higher interest rates, but council flags budget as volatile and rate-dependent.
findings.detail: The council has benefited from 'sustained higher interest rates' providing increased returns on short-term cash holdings. However, the paper explicitly notes the Treasury budget is 'potentially a very volatile budget particularly in the current economic climate and is extremely susceptible to both changes in interest rates.' This is clearly flagged as a one-off benefit.
findings.matters: Shows the council is not in complete freefall (interest rates are helping), but this benefit is temporary. If rates fall, this income disappears and the underlying £7.5m overspend becomes fully visible.
findings.quote: The forecast underspend is largely because of the sustained higher interest rates which has provided the Council with increased levels of interest on its short-term cash flows.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/2027 (First Quarter) to end June 2026
findings.headline: Deputy Chief Executive flags 'longer term uncertainty relating to further increases in demand' and warns council's savings requirements may need to rise.
findings.detail: The finance director notes that demand for services continues to grow and has not stabilized since the budget was approved in February. The recommendation to directors is to 'eliminate deficits in the medium term,' indicating the current trajectory is unsustainable. This is a direct signal from financial leadership that the council's position needs structural improvement.
findings.matters: Signal from the section 151 officer that current forecast is not sustainable and further budget gaps are likely unless demand growth can be arrested. Indicates future savings plans will need to be significantly larger than currently planned.
findings.figures: Homelessness demand +20% (551 vs 459 households); adult care volumes and costs rising; children's placements £0.86m overspend
findings.quote: Whilst the approved Budget 2026/27 originally sought to remedy unavoidable budget pressures, since the budget was approved in February, demand for services continues to place pressure or exacerbate known pressures. Consequently, there remains longer term uncertainty relating to further increases in demand.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/2027 (First Quarter) to end June 2026
findings.headline: Portfolio overspends of £7.5m reduced to reported £0.66m through contingency (£3.8m) and reserve transfers (£3.0m), raising sustainability questions.
findings.detail: Raw portfolio-level overspends total £7.5m. Of this, £3.8m is covered by drawing down Corporate Contingency (treating homelessness, crematorium maintenance, etc. as 'windfall costs'), and £3.0m by planned reserve transfers. This leaves £0.66m reported. Contingency is finite and reserves are being depleted, so this approach is not indefinitely sustainable.
findings.matters: Lenders need to see the true operating position. The use of contingency and reserves to mask underlying overspends signals that the council is not genuinely balanced, and future fiscal pressures could emerge when these tools are exhausted.
findings.figures: £7.5m gross portfolio overspend; £3.8m contingency release; £3.0m reserve transfers; £0.66m net reported
findings.quote: After releases from Contingency (to fund Windfall Costs of £3,847,800) and transfers to and from Reserves, the Council is forecasting an overall overspend of £658,500.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/2027 (First Quarter) to end June 2026
findings.headline: Adult and children's social care costs rising due to volume growth and unit cost inflation: £1.3m adult overspend, £0.86m children's placements, £0.46m transport.
findings.detail: Adult care driven by 'increase in client volumes and average package costs' (£0.9m), staffing/agency inflation (£0.2m), and lost income (£0.26m). Children's services shows sustained cost pressures on care placements and school transport. These are not one-off items but reflect demographic and supply-side pressures.
findings.matters: Aging population plus supplier cost inflation create ongoing budget pressure. Both volumes and unit costs rising simultaneously means this will persist unless service delivery model changes.
findings.figures: Adult care £1.3m overspend; children's placements £0.86m overspend, transport £0.46m overspend
findings.quote: The overspend is primarily due to higher than anticipated care package costs for Adult Care & Support clients within external Residential, Nursing and Domiciliary care placements, due to both an increase in client volumes and average package costs (£0.9m).

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/2027 (First Quarter) to end June 2026
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand up 20% in a year (551 households vs 459), driving £3.2m overspend.
findings.detail: This is the single largest overspend. The council notes insufficient social housing provision to meet demand and has a plan to expand temporary accommodation portfolio, but current demand is far outpacing supply. The paper treats this as a 'windfall cost' but it is clearly structural.
findings.matters: Structural demand growth in homelessness is not cyclical and will persist unless the supply side catches up. This will continue to put pressure on the council's revenue budget and capital plan.
findings.figures: 551 households at Q1 2026/27 vs 459 at Q1 2025/26 (20% increase); £3.2m cost overspend
findings.quote: At the end of Quarter 1 2026/27, 551 households were in temporary accommodation, compared with 459 at the end of Quarter 1 2025/26.
